\chapter{Before, After, and While}
\label{ch:antes-y-despues}
\hlchaptermodality{323}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put two events in order with antes, despues, entonces and mientras, and say that a thing is already done with ya.}

Complete ES-C323-mientras: close todavia no with ya, order two events with antes de and despues de, and join them with mientras.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ya]{ya — two letters, and the opposite of todavía}

\label{lesson:ES-C323-ya}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{right away}, then \emph{not yet}. (\emph{Enseguida}; \emph{todavía no}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{YA}, one beat. The \emph{y} is the same sound that opens \emph{ayuda}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ya} — \textquotedblleft{}already,\textquotedblright{} and sometimes \textquotedblleft{}now.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{iam} meant \emph{already}. Its \emph{i} was said like a \emph{y}, so \emph{iam} was close to \emph{yam}, and the \emph{m} dropped. Two letters left.

An English speaker has been carrying this word without knowing it. French wore \emph{iam} down to \emph{ja} and put \emph{de} in front of it: \textbf{déjà} — \emph{already}. English borrowed the phrase whole and never translated it. Every time somebody says \textbf{déjà vu}, \emph{already seen}, the \emph{jà} in the middle is \emph{ya}.

Now set it against the word you just learned. \emph{Todavía} says the thing has not stopped. \emph{Ya} says the thing has arrived. \emph{Todavía no} is \emph{not yet}; \emph{ya} is \emph{it's done}. They are the two ends of one line, and Spanish speakers swap between them constantly.

\emph{Ya} also does a job English needs a whole tone of voice for. Said alone — \emph{¡ya!} — it means \emph{that's enough}, \emph{stop there}. Two letters, and the timing is the whole message.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The shortest word in the run, and the one that closes a door.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ya}
  \item \emph{ya está}
  \item \emph{todavía no — ya}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which borrowed French phrase hides \emph{ya} inside it? (\emph{Déjà vu} — already seen.) And what is the opposite of \emph{todavía no}? (\emph{Ya}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[entonces]{entonces — pointing at a time the way you point at a chair}

\label{lesson:ES-C323-entonces}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{still}, then \emph{already}. (\emph{Todavía}; \emph{ya}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en-TON-ces}, stress in the middle, and a clear \emph{s} on the end. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{entonces} — \textquotedblleft{}then.\textquotedblright{}

Inside it are two pieces you can nearly see. \emph{En} is the \emph{en} you know, from Latin \textbf{in}. \textbf{Tunc} was Latin for \emph{at that time}. \emph{In tunc} — \emph{at that time} — ran together, and Spanish added an \emph{-s} on the end, the way it likes to.

\emph{Tunc} was itself built out of something older and much shorter: the pointing stem that English still runs on. \textbf{That}, \textbf{there}, \textbf{then}, \textbf{the} — all of them are that one small sound, put to work in different directions. So Spanish \emph{entonces} and English \emph{then} are cousins, arriving by different roads from a word whose only job was to point away from here.

That is what \emph{entonces} does. It points at a time the way \emph{ese} points at a chair. It is also the word that carries an argument along — \emph{entonces, ¿qué?}, \emph{so, what then?} — because \emph{and at that time} is how a story keeps moving.

Two other jobs, one word: \emph{entonces} is a \emph{then} on a clock, and a \emph{so} in a sentence.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word that can push a conversation forward when you have run out of others.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{entonces}
  \item \emph{entonces, ¿qué?}
  \item \emph{ya — entonces}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin words are inside \emph{entonces}? (\emph{In} and \emph{tunc} — at that time.) Which English words share that old pointing sound? (\emph{That}, \emph{there}, \emph{then}, \emph{the}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[antes]{antes — the one that goes in front}

\label{lesson:ES-C323-antes}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{already}, then \emph{then}. (\emph{Ya}; \emph{entonces}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{AN-tes}, stress on the first beat, and the \emph{s} on the end is not swallowed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{antes} — \textquotedblleft{}before.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{ante} meant \emph{in front of}, in space first and in time afterwards. The \emph{-s} on the end is Spanish, not Latin: it is the ending Spanish keeps hanging on words that say \emph{when}. You saw it on \emph{entonces}, and it is coming again.

English took \emph{ante} and mostly left it alone. An \textbf{antechamber} is the room in front of the room. To \textbf{antedate} is to be earlier than. In a card game you \textbf{ante up} — you put in before you play. \textbf{Antique} and \textbf{ancient} are both \emph{ante} grown old, which is what they mean.

The best one is \textbf{ancestor}. Latin \textbf{antecessor} is \emph{ante} plus \emph{cedere}, \emph{to go}: \textbf{one who went before}. Not an old relative — a walker who was on the road first.

To say \emph{before something}, Spanish puts \emph{de} after it: \emph{antes de}. The word by itself just means \emph{earlier}: \emph{antes, no} — \emph{not before now}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Half of a pair. The other half arrives next.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{antes}
  \item \emph{antes de comer}
  \item \emph{entonces — antes}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is an \emph{antecessor}, word for word? (One who went before.) Which other \emph{when} word carries the same \emph{-s} on the end? (\emph{Entonces}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[después]{después — three words that stopped being three}

\label{lesson:ES-C323-despues}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{then}, then \emph{before}. (\emph{Entonces}; \emph{antes}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{des-PUÉS}, stress on the last beat — the written accent says so, and the \emph{ué} is one glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{después} — \textquotedblleft{}after,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}afterwards.\textquotedblright{}

This one is a pile-up. Latin had \textbf{post}, \emph{after}. Speakers put \textbf{ex} in front of it for emphasis, then \textbf{de} in front of that, and \emph{de ex post} was said so often it fused: \emph{despost}, \emph{depués}, \emph{después}. Three words to say one thing, and now nobody hears the seams.

The \textbf{post} is the piece English kept. To \textbf{postpone} is to place after. A \textbf{postscript} is written after. Something \textbf{posterior} is at the back. \textbf{Post-war} is after the war. And \textbf{preposterous} is \emph{prae} plus \emph{posterus} — \emph{before-after} — a thing with its front where its back should be, which is a very exact way of saying \emph{absurd}.

Set the pair together now. \emph{Antes} and \emph{después}. Both are Latin place-words that learned to talk about time; both end in that same Spanish \emph{-s}, like \emph{entonces}. To hang either on a thing, you use \emph{de}: \emph{antes de}, \emph{después de}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A pair that can put two events in order without a clock.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{después}
  \item \emph{después de comer}
  \item \emph{antes — después}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many Latin words are inside \emph{después}? (Three — \emph{de}, \emph{ex}, \emph{post}.) What does \emph{preposterous} mean, piece by piece? (Before-after, back to front.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mientras]{mientras — twenty words, and one ending they share}

\label{lesson:ES-C323-mientras}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{before eating}, then \emph{after eating}. (\emph{Antes de comer}; \emph{después de comer}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{MIEN-tras}, stress on the first beat. The \emph{ie} is one glide, as in \emph{tiempo}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mientras} — \textquotedblleft{}while.\textquotedblright{}

Latin said \textbf{dum interim}: \emph{while, in the meantime}. \textbf{Interim} is \emph{inter}, \emph{between}, with an ending — the time in between. Old Spanish had it as \emph{demientre}; the pieces slid, the \emph{-s} arrived, and \emph{mientras} was left.

That \emph{inter} is one of the most visible Latin pieces in English. An \textbf{interim} report covers the time between. An \textbf{interval} is the gap between. Something \textbf{interior} is between the walls. \textbf{International} is between nations. And \textbf{meanwhile} is English building the same idea out of its own bricks.

Now the ending, because it is the point of this chapter. Take the four together: \emph{entonces}, \emph{antes}, \emph{después}, \emph{mientras}. Every one of them ends in \emph{-s}, and not one of them is more than one thing. That \emph{-s} is not a plural. Spanish grew a habit of finishing its \emph{when}-words that way, and once you hear it you will spot the next one before anyone explains it.

\emph{Mientras} joins two things happening at once: \emph{mientras como} — while I eat.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Twenty words. Ten name what courtesy is made of; ten put things in time — a night behind you, a week to count in, a place in the day, the next instant, a thing not finished, a thing already done, a \emph{then}, a \emph{before}, an \emph{after}, and a \emph{while}. Between them you can say a good deal more at a door than \emph{hasta luego}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mientras}
  \item \emph{mientras como}
  \item \emph{antes — después — mientras}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{inter} mean? (Between.) What do \emph{entonces}, \emph{antes}, \emph{después} and \emph{mientras} all share on the end? (An \emph{-s} that is not a plural.)
\end{tcolorbox}
